doc.title: Jim Galloway interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: Dance-crazy Glasgow and dancing to jazz
summary: Glasgow's dance halls supported many big bands until television; the dancing styles and his attitude to dancers.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: So were you playing — still in Scotland now — was it for dances or jazz clubs?

Glasgow at that time was dance crazy. There were I don’t know how many dance halls going five, six nights a week in Glasgow at that time. I knew that there was employment for four or five big bands, six nights a week.
And then of course the onslaught of television killed it, as it’s done to stuff all over the place.
The dancing they were doing, was it the dances of — let me rephrase the question — were they doing the lindy hop and all that kind of stuff or was it more—

Most of it was pretty straight ahead sort of body contact dancing, old fashioned dancing. And there were always a few people, especially in a jazz club, who would be into doing some jitterbug dancing.

And I’ve never minded that, because the music is essentially a communication with people. And in its origins a lot of people danced to the music. So it’s never been a problem for me to have people dancing.

Yeah. Sometimes it helps. You can see what they respond to and shift your tempos to really get the thing happening. So early 60s, was the decision to come over here a long one? Was it something that you thought about for a long time?
